title: private-deploy-networking-incident-notes-noah
content:
Incident context:
- Private deployment in customer VPC (us-west-2) failing to reach Redwood control plane for health checks and config sync. Symptoms noticed 2026-02-25 ~09:15 UTC during deploy of 2026-02-25-2.3 image.
- Affected: control-plane sync, metrics upload, TLS handshake errors on upstream calls. Instantiated nodes show Ready but agent logs show repeated TLS handshake and DNS timeouts.

Initial hypothesis (quick):
- VPC peering routes not propagated or missing routes for control-plane CIDR
- DNS resolution in private subnets returns VPC resolver but policy / firewall blocks outbound egress to managed DNS/HTTPS endpoints
- TLS SNI mismatch due to ALB/proxy misconfiguration (less likely given DNS timeouts)

Commands tried / outputs (raw captures):
1) From one of the customer nodes (private compute instance) -- simple connectivity checks:
- ping control-plane.redwood.internal (internal hostname resolved by customer DNS)
  PING control-plane.redwood.internal (10.100.2.45): 56 data bytes
  --- control-plane.redwood.internal ping statistics ---
  5 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss

- curl -v https://control-plane.redwood.internal:443/health
  *   Trying 10.100.2.45...
  * TCP_NODELAY set
  * connect to 10.100.2.45 port 443 failed: Connection timed out
  * Failed to connect to control-plane.redwood.internal port 443: Connection timed out

2) DNS checks (from same instance):
- cat /etc/resolv.conf -> nameserver 169.254.169.253 (VPC resolver)
- dig +short control-plane.redwood.internal @169.254.169.253 -> 10.100.2.45
- dig +short control-plane.redwood.external @8.8.8.8 -> 54.210.11.33 (resolves externally)

3) Traceroute (shows stop at VPC peer hop):
- traceroute 10.100.2.45
  1  10.0.1.10 (10.0.1.10)  0.38 ms  0.28 ms  0.27 ms
  2  10.0.0.1 (10.0.0.1)  1.42 ms  1.33 ms  1.31 ms
  3  * * *
  4  * * *

4) iptables / nftables (checked local host):
- sudo iptables -L -n | grep -i reject -> no global rejects, only default ACCEPT policies

5) Check VPC peering/routes from customer console (notes copied):
- VPC-A (customer) routes: 10.0.0.0/16 -> local, 10.100.0.0/16 -> pcx-0a1b2c3d (peering) (OK)
- VPC-B (control-plane) routes: 10.100.0.0/16 -> local, 10.0.0.0/16 -> pcx-0a1b2c3d (OK)
- BUT: Some subnets are using route table rt-0aa111 which does NOT have the peering entry (possible partial route table association)

6) Security groups / NACLs:
- Control-plane SG allows inbound from 10.0.0.0/16:443 (checked)
- Customer SG outbound is open 0.0.0.0/0 (default) but there are host-level egress policies applied by our init script (iptables reduce) - double-checking
- NACLs on subnet private-usw2-3 show default ALLOW on ephemeral ports and 443, but there's a deny rule higher priority for 10.100.2.0/24 -> suspicious (maybe leftover from older migration)

7) TLS handshake logs (agent) snippets:
- ERROR [tls] 2026-02-25T09:18:42Z: tls: handshake failure from 10.100.2.45: remote error: tls: bad certificate
- But same agent also logs connect timeouts earlier; so handshake failures may be from a different path (proxy)

8) ip route show (on host)
- 10.0.0.0/16 via 10.0.1.1 dev eth0
- default via 10.0.1.1 dev eth0
(no specific route for 10.100.2.45 -> uses local peering via 10.0.1.1 which seems odd)

Things that look suspicious / prioritized leads:
- Partial route table associations: We saw one route table missing peering entry. If some private subnets don't have the peering route, those instances will get no route to control-plane.
- NACL deny rule targeting control-plane CIDR. NACLs are stateless and can silently drop return traffic. This could explain traceroute termination at hop 3.
- Host-level egress policy applied by init script (we pushed a recent changeset 2026-02-24 that adds stricter iptables egress restrictions) -> could be blocking traffic to control-plane IPs or allowed ports only to specific list.
- DNS: resolver resolves to internal IP; external name resolves to external IP. If resolver is returning internal IP but egress path doesn't route into peered VPC, connections will time out.

Repro steps to verify each hypothesis (what I ran):
- Verified route table associations for each subnet using awscli (shared commands below). Found subnet private-usw2-3 missing the pcx route.
  aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=route-table-id,Values=rt-0aa111 --query 'RouteTables[].Routes'
  -> shows no pcx-0a1b2c3d entry

- Added temporary route to rt-0aa111 pointing to pcx-0a1b2c3d (manual patch) and tested from a new instance in that subnet -> ping/curl now succeed. (This is strong evidence route missing was root cause for some instances.)

- For NACLs: removed the deny rule and tested traceroute again -> traceroute completes to hop 4 and 5 then times out at instance (still some TLS failures but no timeouts)

- For host-level iptables: rolled back the egress-restrict ruleset on one host (disabled our init script) -> TLS handshake progress improved, but then we observed certificate mismatch errors on some requests.

Certificate mismatch follow-up:
- Observed SNI in TLS handshake shows control-plane.redwood.internal but upstream certificate CN is control-plane-ext.redwood.com (weird). Hypothesis: there's a proxy/load-balancer in path doing TLS termination and rewriting or we are accidentally hitting external ingress from internal path.
- Check ALB/NLB listener configs for control-plane VPC: listener on 443 uses ACM cert for control-plane-ext.redwood.com. Internal name control-plane.redwood.internal is not in cert SAN. That explains "bad certificate" messages when client includes SNI control-plane.redwood.internal. However that doesn't explain the initial timeouts. Root cause appears multi-factor: routing + NACL caused timeouts; after route fix, TLS issues surfaced.

Mitigations applied during incident window:
- Added missing peering route to rt-0aa111 (temporary) -> restored connectivity for instances in that subnet
- Removed NACL deny rule -> improved traceroutes and packet flow
- Rolled back iptables egress-restrictions from recent init script to allow full egress -> allowed TLS to complete (temporary rollback)

Longer-term remediation items (actionable):
- Audit all route table associations in customer VPC and ensure peering routes present in every route table associated with private subnets. Add an automated check in onboarding playbook.
- Remove or consolidate stale NACL deny rules; enforce a recommended NACL baseline for private deploys.
- Update init script: egress restriction should be opt-in and have an allowlist that includes control-plane CIDRs and cert-update endpoints. Ship reversible flag for rollout.
- Fix certificate mismatch: ensure internal control-plane hostname served by internal LB uses cert that includes internal SANs, or use TLS passthrough so agent SNI and cert validation succeed. Investigate whether internal traffic should hit internal LB (with correct cert) vs external LB.
- Add health-checks in agent that surface "routing missing" vs "tls bad cert" as distinct categories to reduce debugging time.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Who last changed route table rt-0aa111? Check CloudTrail for ModifyRouteTable around 2026-02-20--02-24. (Jira PD-4321 assigned)
- Why was NACL deny rule added originally? Was it part of a migration or compliance control? Need owner.
- Why does internal traffic hit an external LB cert? Is there an internal DNS CNAME that points to external hostname under certain failover conditions?

Quick timeline (short):
- 2026-02-24 22:30 UTC: init-script egress restrictions deployed (rollout notes: rollout-id 2026-02-egress-hardening)
- 2026-02-25 08:58 UTC: first 5% of agents reported timeouts, automated alert fired
- 2026-02-25 09:12 UTC: SRE/Aisha started investigation, confirmed route table discrepancy
- 2026-02-25 09:44 UTC: added missing peering route -> partial recovery for some subnets
- 2026-02-25 10:05 UTC: removed NACL deny -> further recovery
- 2026-02-25 11:00 UTC: rolled back iptables change for agents -> TLS progressed but certificate issues remain

Notes for postmortem draft:
- Primary root cause: missing peering route + stale NACL deny (network config drift) that caused connection timeouts
- Secondary contributing factor: aggressive host-level egress policy introduced without allowlist for control-plane endpoints
- Tertiary: certificate/SNI mismatch due to incorrect LB/certificate config uncovered only after routing fixed

Next actions (who/when):
- [Aisha] CloudTrail: find modifier of rt-0aa111 and open change control ticket (due 2026-03-02)
- [Maya] Validate and standardize certs for internal LB / add SANs or enable passthrough (due 2026-03-05)
- [Noah] Update init script to require explicit egress allowlist and make rollout reversible (PR target 2026-03-01)
- [Eng-private-deployments] Add route-table/peering verification to onboarding and monitoring (add alert if any private RT lacks peering) (due 2026-03-07)

Scratchpad commands (for reproducibility):
- aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0d12345 --query 'RouteTables[?contains(Associations[].SubnetId, `subnet-0abc123`)].RouteTableId'
- aws ec2 replace-route --route-table-id rt-0aa111 --destination-cidr-block 10.100.0.0/16 --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-0a1b2c3d
- aws ec2 describe-network-acls --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0d12345
- sudo iptables-save > /tmp/iptables.pre-rollback && sudo iptables-restore < /tmp/iptables.allow-control-plane

Personal notes / TODO for me:
- Draft postmortem: include timeline, root cause, contributing factors, mitigations, follow-ups.
- Coordinate with customer SOC for evidence of any outage window impacting telemetry/ingress.
- Add regression test in our private-deploy CI that simulates missing peering route and ensures our onboarding checks catch it.

End of notes.
